parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-isko via Old Polish *-isko.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ба́чити, ба́чыти (báčiti, báčyti), from Old Polish baczyć (“to see, to notice, to look”).
From Old Ruthenian блюзнѣ́ръ (bljuzně́r), which was borrowed from Old Polish bluźnierz.
Borrowed from Old Polish bryże, from Old High German brize, from Middle French frise.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian бу́да (búda), from Old Polish buda, from Middle High German buode.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian вада (vada, “flaw, slander”), the sense "'flaw'" is probably a semantic loan from Old Polish wada, from Proto-Slavic *vada. By surface analysis, ва́дити (vádyty) + -а (-a).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian вспакъ (vspak), possibly from Old Polish wspak, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *opakъ.

parole.significato: to hold back, to restrain, to contain, to check, to subdue, to repress, to temper, to withhold
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian гамовати (hamovati) (since the early XVI), from Old Polish hamować, from Middle High German hamen, from Old High German *hamōn. Compare modern German hemmen, from Proto-West Germanic *hammjan, whence also English hem.

Inherited from Middle Ukrainian гетьманъ m (hetʹman), гетманъ m (hetman), from Old Polish hethman m, probably from Middle High German houbetman, heuptman (“commander”), from houbet, heupt (“head”), related to Latin caput (“head”), + Middle High German man (“man”). Compare Modern Polish hetman m and

parole.significato: to care, to look after, to take care
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian дба́ти (dbáti), judging by its geographic spread, likely borrowed from Old Polish dbać, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *dъbati. Cognate with Belarusian дбаць (dbacʹ), Czech dbát.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian зекгаръ (zegar), дзикгаръ (dzigar), from Old Polish zegar, zygar, from Middle High German seigære. Compare Polish zegar.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian до́бре (dóbre), from Old Polish dobrze, from Proto-Slavic *dobrě, from Proto-Slavic *dobrъ. Doublet of добрі́ (dobrí). See Ukrainian добрий.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian довтепъ (dovtep), probably from Old Polish dowcip, ultimately from Old Czech dovtip, possibly from Proto-Slavic *těpati. Forms such as Old Ruthenian довципъ (dovcip) were definitely borrowed from Polish.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian дѧ́ковати (djákovati, “to thank”), from Old Polish dziękować, from Old High German dankōn, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þankōną.

parole.significato: the general public, the collective, society
parole.testo: From Old Polish zahałem, whence Polish zagałem.

parole.significato: to agree to, to consent to
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian згодитисꙗ (zhoditisja, “to agree, to reconcile”), likely from Old Polish zgodzić się, compare etymology 1. By surface analysis, зго́дити (zhódyty, “to bring together, to convince”) + -ся (-sja).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian зле (zle), from Old Polish źle, from Proto-Slavic *zъlě, from Proto-Slavic *zъlъ. Doublet of зло (zlo).
Borrowed from Old Polish złoty. Doublet of золоти́й (zolotýj).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian зрада (zrada), borrowed from Old Polish zdrada.

Inherited from Middle Ukrainian кушнѣръ (kušnir), from earlier кушнеръ (kušner), from Old Polish kusznierz, from Middle High German kürsenære, from Old High German kursināri, from Old High German kursina, from Proto-Slavic *kъrzьno, whence Ukrainian ко́рзно (kórzno).
Uncertain. Possibly borrowed from Old Polish ława.

parole.significato: to torture, to torment, to rack, to excruciate (inflict severe physical pain or mental suffering on)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian мордова́ти (mordováti, “to torture, to torment”), from Old Polish mordować (“to murder”), from Middle High German morden, mörden, mürden (“to murder”), from Old High German morden, murden (“to murder”), from Proto-West Germanic *murþijan (“to murder”), from Proto-Germani

Inherited from Old Ruthenian му́сити (músiti), from Old Polish musić, from Middle High German müeȥen, from Old High German muoȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *mōtan, from Proto-Germanic *mōtaną (whence German müssen and English must). Compare loans from the same source Belarusian му́сіць (músicʹ), Cze
Inherited from Old Ruthenian насѣньє (nasěnʹje), from Old Polish nasienie, from Proto-Slavic *nasěnьje.

parole.significato: to destroy, to obliterate, to annihilate, to eliminate
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian нищити (niščiti, “to destroy, to devastate, to ruin, to impoverish”), possibly from Old Polish niszczyć, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *niščiti. By surface analysis, (dated) ни́щий (nýščyj) + -ити (-yty).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian огуро́къ (ohurók) (since Skorina, 1519), semi-calque of Old Polish ogurek (since 1394, modern Polish ogórek), from Byzantine Greek ἀγγούριον (angoúrion) or a related form.

parole.significato: to receive, to get, to obtain
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian одержати (oderžati), from Old Polish odzierżeć, which is a partial calque of Latin obtineo. Equivalent to о- (o-) + де́ржати (déržaty). Compare Russian одержа́ть (oderžátʹ).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian осо́ба (osóba, “person, appearance, species, hypostasis”), possibly borrowed from Old Polish osoba.

parole.significato: lord, master, mister, sir (a general honorific title)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian панъ (pan), from Old East Slavic панъ (panŭ), from Old Polish pan, from Proto-Slavic *gъpanъ.
Inherited from Middle Ukrainian па́ни f sg (pány), from Old East Slavic пани f sg (pani), from Old Polish pani f sg, from Proto-Slavic *gъpanьji f sg.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian парсуна (parsuna), from Old Polish parsuna, ultimately from Latin persona. Doublet of персо́на (persóna).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian передмѣстье, предмѣстье (peredměstʹje, predměstʹje), from Old Polish przedmieście. By surface analysis, перед- (pered-) + мі́сто (místo) + -я (-ja). Compare Russian предме́стье (predméstʹje), Belarusian прадме́сце (pradmjéscje).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian пыха, пиха (pyxa, pixa), from Old Polish pycha, from Old Czech pýcha, deverbal from Old Czech pýchati, from Proto-Slavic *pyxati (“to puff”). For an identical development compare Ukrainian наду́тий (nadútyj), Russian надме́нный, наду́тый (nadménnyj, nadútyj).

Inherited from Middle Ukrainian повиненъ, повыненъ (povynen, povynen), from Old East Slavic повиньнъ (povinĭnŭ), the sense "obligated, ought" may have been reinforced by Old Polish powinien, as it was uncommon in Old East Slavic. By surface analysis, по (po) + вина́ (vyná) + -ен (-en). Cognate with
Inherited from Old Ruthenian пра́ца (práca), from Old Polish praca, from Old Czech prácě, from Proto-Slavic *porťa.

parole.significato: privilege (a particular benefit, advantage, or favor; a right or immunity enjoyed by some but not others; a prerogative…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian привилеи (privilei), привилей (privilej), from Old Polish przywilej, from Latin prīvilēgium.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian ра́да (ráda), from Old East Slavic ра́да (ráda), from Old Polish rada, from Old Czech rada, from Middle High German rāt, from Old High German rāt, from Proto-West Germanic *rād, from Proto-Germanic *rēdaz.
First attested in Old Ruthenian респектъ (respekt), from Old Polish respekt, from Latin respectus. Probably reintroduced later by German Respekt and in modern sense ("props") from English respect.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian роди́на (rodína, “family, homeland”), the sense "family" is a semantic loan from Old Polish rodzina (“family”). By surface analysis, род- (rod-) + -ина (-yna).

parole.significato: diverse, heterogenous, multifarious, manifold, motley, various (consisting of many different elements)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian розмаи́тый (rozmaítyj), from Old Polish rozmaity, probably from unattested dialectal West Slavic *orzmaj, from Proto-Slavic *orzmajati, from *majati.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian роспачъ, роспачь (rospač, rospačʹ), from Old Polish rozpacz, from Proto-Slavic *orzpačь. Compare Belarusian ро́спач (róspač).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian скри́ня, скры́ня (skrínja, skrýnja), from Old Polish skrzynia, from Proto-Slavic *skrini, from Old High German skrīni, from Latin scrīnium.

parole.significato: deadly, lethal, fatal, mortal (resulting in death)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian смерте́льный (smertélʹnyj), from Old Polish śmiertelny, ultimately from Old Czech smrtedlný.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian спо́собъ (spósob), most likely from Old Polish sposób, which itself is possibly from Old Czech zpósob (maybe only influenced semantically), from Proto-Slavic *sъposobъ.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian сумнєнїє (sumnjenije) (with semantic loan from Old Polish sąmnienie / sumnienie (“conscience”)), from Old East Slavic сумьнѣниѥ (sumĭněnije, “doubt, hesitation”). Compare Belarusian сумле́нне (sumljénnje, “conscience”), Polish sumienie (“conscience”) but Russian сомне́ни

parole.significato: to hit (to manage to touch (a target) in the right place)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian тра́пити (trápiti), from Old Polish trapić, trafić, from Middle High German treffan, from Old High German treffan, from Proto-West Germanic *drepan, from Proto-Germanic *drepaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreb-, *dʰrebʰ- (“to grind; crush; kill”), whence also Ukrainian

parole.significato: to last, to endure, to continue
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian трыва́ти (tryváti), from Old Polish trwać, from Proto-Slavic *trъvàti.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian триво́жити (trivóžiti), from earlier трво́жити (trvóžiti), from Old Polish trwożyć, from Proto-Slavic *trъvožiti. By surface analysis, триво́га (tryvóha) + -ити (-yty).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian тримати (trimati), from Old Polish trzymać, from Proto-Slavic *trimati.

parole.significato: to use, to make use of
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian ужива́ти (uživáti), possibly influenced by or borrowed from Old Polish używać. By surface analysis, у- (u-) + жива́ти (žyváty).

parole.significato: to use, to make use of
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian ужи́ти (užíti), possibly influenced by or borrowed from Old Polish użyć. By surface analysis, у- (u-) + жи́ти (žýty).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian ꙋчинокъ (učinok), possibly from Old Polish uczynek, however native derivation from Old East Slavic ꙋчинити (učiniti, “to do”) is possible. By surface analysis, учини́ти (učynýty) + -ок (-ok)
Inherited from Old Ruthenian цыбу́лѧ, цибу́лѧ (cybúlja, cibúlja), from Old Polish cybula, from Middle High German zibolle, zebülle, zwibole, from Late Latin cepulla, from Latin cepa.
Inherited from Old East Slavic школа (škola), from Old Polish szkoła (“school”), ultimately from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).
Borrowed from Old Polish śpiegun.

parole.significato: to unite, to bond, to bring together
parole.testo: Probably inherited from Old Ruthenian еднати (ednati, “to reconcile, to ask for, to appease”) with the later semantic shift to "to unite", ultimately from Old Polish jednać. By surface analysis, (dialectal) єден (jeden) + -а́ти (-áty).
From Middle Ukrainian кгвалтъ (gvalt), гвалтъ (hvalt), ґвалтъ (gvalt), through Old Polish gwałt (Polish gwałt), from Middle High German gewalt (“strength, power”).
